Ruth: Faithfulness and Redemption

Reference: The Book of Ruth

Big Idea: God honors our faithfulness, and He provides a Redeemer to rescue us when we cannot rescue ourselves.

Teacher Quick Reference

⏱️
Lesson: Ruth: Faithfulness and Redemption
Scripture: The Book of Ruth
Big Idea: God honors our faithfulness, and He provides a Redeemer to rescue us when we cannot rescue ourselves.
Three Main Points:
  1. Naomi lost her husband and sons in a foreign land and was left with nothing.
  2. Ruth loyally refused to leave Naomi, saying, 'Your God will be my God.'
  3. Ruth gathered leftover grain (gleaned) in the field of a kind man named Boaz.
  4. Boaz acted as their 'Kinsman-Redeemer' to buy back their land and marry Ruth.
  5. Ruth became the great-grandmother of King David, and an ancestor of Jesus.
Activity: The Gleaning Game
Memory Verse: Ruth 1:16
Take-Home Truth:
"God loves my faithful choices, and Jesus is the Redeemer who rescues me."

Teacher Preparation

Before class:

  • Read the Book of Ruth (BSB). It is only 4 chapters and reads like a beautiful short story.
  • Familiarize yourself with the concept of the Kinsman-Redeemer (a close relative who had the legal right to buy back land that a poor relative had lost, and to marry a childless widow to continue the family name).
  • Prepare the materials (tape, cotton balls/paper) for The Gleaning Game.
  • Write the memory verse on the board.
  • Decide which age adaptation will work best for your classroom.

[!IMPORTANT] A note for the teacher The book of Ruth is a masterclass in how God works through ordinary, faithful people. There are no burning bushes, parted seas, or booming voices from heaven in this story. God’s providence is seen through the quiet, everyday kindness of Ruth and Boaz. Emphasize to the children that they don’t have to do something “famous” to be used by God; small acts of kindness and loyalty are powerful in God’s hands.

Opening Activity: Leaving Everything Behind

Ask the children: “If you had to move to a brand new country tomorrow, and you could only pack one small backpack, what would you bring?”

Allow the children to share a few answers. Then ask: “What would you miss the most about your home?”

Explain: “Moving far away is really hard, especially if you have to leave your friends and your home behind. Today, we are going to learn about a woman who left her country, her friends, and everything she knew behind, just because she wanted to take care of someone she loved.”

The Bible Story

1. Tragedy in Moab

During a terrible famine in Israel, a man named Elimelech took his wife, Naomi, and their two sons to live in a foreign country called Moab. While they were there, the two sons married Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth.

But then, terrible tragedy struck. Naomi’s husband died. Then, ten years later, both of her sons died too. In the ancient world, if a woman had no husband and no sons, she had no way to make money or protect herself. Naomi was heartbroken, poor, and alone.

Naomi decided to travel back to her home in Bethlehem (in Israel) because she heard the famine was over. She told her two daughters-in-law to stay in Moab and find new husbands. Orpah cried and kissed Naomi goodbye. But Ruth refused to leave.

2. Ruth’s Choice

Ruth made one of the most beautiful promises in the entire Bible. She clung to Naomi and said:

“Do not urge me to leave you or to turn back from following you. For where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16, BSB)

Ruth chose to leave her own country to follow the one true God, and to take care of Naomi. So the two widows traveled back to Bethlehem together, arriving right at the beginning of the barley harvest.

3. Gleaning in the Fields

Naomi and Ruth were very poor and had no food. But God had given the Israelites a special law. Farmers were not allowed to harvest the very edges of their fields, and they couldn’t pick up the grain they dropped. They had to leave it for the poor people to gather. This was called “gleaning.”

Ruth went out to glean, and she “happened” to end up in a field belonging to a wealthy, kind man named Boaz.

When Boaz saw Ruth working so hard, he asked who she was. His workers told him how she had left her homeland to take care of Naomi. Boaz was amazed by her loyalty. He told Ruth to stay in his fields where she would be safe, and he even secretly told his workers to drop extra grain on purpose for her to find!

4. The Kinsman-Redeemer

When Ruth came home with massive amounts of grain, Naomi was overjoyed. She realized that Boaz was a close relative of her dead husband. In Israel, a close relative could be a “Kinsman-Redeemer.” This was a family hero who could step in, pay off debts, buy back lost land, and rescue a widow.

Naomi told Ruth to go to the threshing floor at night, uncover Boaz’s feet while he slept, and lie down. This sounds strange to us, but it was an ancient, respectful way of asking him to spread his blanket over her—meaning, asking him to protect her and marry her.

When Boaz woke up, Ruth said:

“Spread the corner of your garment over your maidservant, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” (Ruth 3:9, BSB)

Boaz was honored. He promised to do everything he could to rescue them.

5. The Big Surprise

Boaz went to the town gate and legally bought back all the land that belonged to Naomi’s family. He became the Kinsman-Redeemer, and he took Ruth to be his wife. God blessed them with a baby boy named Obed. Naomi, who had been so sad and empty, was full of joy again as she held her new grandson.

But the story doesn’t end there! The Bible gives us a big surprise at the very end of the book. Obed grew up and had a son named Jesse. And Jesse had a son named… David. Ruth, the poor, foreign widow who left everything to be faithful to God, became the great-grandmother of King David! And hundreds of years later, Jesus Christ Himself would be born into this exact same family.

The Deeper Meaning

The concept of the Kinsman-Redeemer is a perfect picture of Jesus. To be a Kinsman-Redeemer, a man had to meet three requirements:

  1. He had to be a relative (Kinsman).
  2. He had to have the ability to pay the debt.
  3. He had to be willing to do it.

Look at how Jesus is our ultimate Redeemer!

  1. He became our relative: Jesus left heaven and became a human being so He could be one of us.
  2. He had the ability to pay: Because Jesus lived a perfect, sinless life, only He could pay the debt for our sins.
  3. He was willing to do it: Jesus willingly laid down His life on the cross because He loves us.

Boaz redeemed Ruth from poverty. Jesus redeemed us from sin!

Three Things to Remember

1. Loyalty is Powerful

Ruth could have taken the easy way out and stayed in Moab, but she chose the hard, faithful path. God loves when we are loyal to our friends, our family, and to Him. Teacher Question: When is it hard to be a loyal friend?

2. God Works Through Small Kindness

Boaz didn’t have to leave extra grain for Ruth, but he chose to be generous. God used Boaz’s small acts of kindness to literally save Naomi and Ruth from starving. Teacher Question: What is a small act of kindness you could do this week that might be a big deal to someone else?

3. Jesus is Our Redeemer

Just like Ruth and Naomi couldn’t rescue themselves from their poverty, we cannot rescue ourselves from sin. We need a Redeemer, and Jesus is the perfect one. Teacher Question: Why did Jesus have to become a human being to save us?

Age Adaptations

Preschool (Ages 3-5)

Younger Children

For younger children (ages 5–7), focus on Ruth’s loyalty and Boaz’s kindness.

Simplified concepts:

  • Naomi was very sad because her family died and she had no food.
  • Ruth was a good, loyal friend. She promised to stay with Naomi forever.
  • Ruth went to pick up leftover food in a field.
  • A nice man named Boaz owned the field. He shared his food and protected Ruth.
  • God used Boaz to rescue Naomi and Ruth, and eventually, Ruth had a baby who was in the same family as Jesus!

Developmentally appropriate questions:

  • Did Ruth leave Naomi when things got sad and hard? (No).
  • Was Boaz mean and greedy, or nice and generous? (Nice and generous).
  • Who takes care of us and rescues us? (Jesus).
Upper Elementary (Grades 4-6)

Older Children

For older children (ages 8–11), focus heavily on the theological concept of the Kinsman-Redeemer.

Deeper discussion: Help pre-teens understand the legal/historical concept of the Kinsman-Redeemer so they can fully grasp the beauty of what Jesus did on the cross.

Discussion Scenarios:

  • Scenario 1: Imagine you owe a million dollars and you have zero in your bank account. If your best friend wants to help you, but they also have zero dollars, can they redeem (rescue) you? (No, they lack the ability). What if a billionaire stranger comes to town, but he doesn’t care about you? (He lacks the willingness). Jesus had both!
  • Concept: Notice that Ruth was a Moabitess (a foreigner). She wasn’t an Israelite. By making her the great-grandmother of King David, God was proving that His love and salvation are for everyone, not just one specific group of people.

Discussion Questions

Understanding

  1. Why did Naomi and her family move to Moab in the first place?
  2. What did Ruth tell Naomi when Naomi told her to go back home?
  3. What is “gleaning”?
  4. What nice things did Boaz do for Ruth when she was in his field?
  5. Who was Ruth’s famous great-grandson?

Thinking

  1. Why was it dangerous and difficult for Ruth to go to Bethlehem with Naomi?
  2. Do you think it was a “coincidence” that Ruth ended up in Boaz’s field? Why or why not?
  3. What were the three things a Kinsman-Redeemer had to be? (A relative, able to pay, willing).
  4. How is Jesus like Boaz? How are we like Ruth?

Personal Application

  1. Have you ever had a friend stick with you when you were going through a hard time? How did it feel?
  2. How can you show the kind of loyalty that Ruth showed?
  3. Why does knowing that Jesus is your Redeemer make you want to follow Him?

Activity Time

Activity Resource: The Gleaning Game View Standalone →

Materials:

  • Lots of small items to scatter on the floor (e.g., cotton balls, crumpled pieces of yellow paper, or yellow blocks) to represent 'grain'.
  • A basket or bucket for each team.
  • Masking tape or painter's tape to mark off areas.

Templates:

📄 Gleaning Game Instruction Card

Purpose

To teach the biblical concept of gleaning (God’s command to leave the edges of the fields for the poor and foreigners) while providing a high-energy activity.

Setup

  1. Use the tape to mark a large square in the center of the room. This is the “Main Field.”
  2. Scatter the vast majority of the “grain” (cotton balls or paper) inside the taped square.
  3. Scatter a small amount of “grain” outside the tape, around the edges of the room.
  4. Divide the children into two groups: “The Harvesters” (a larger group) and “The Gleaners” (a smaller group, maybe 2 or 3 children).

Exact Instructions

  1. Explain the rules to the children before they move:
    • The Harvesters are only allowed to gather grain inside the taped square. They cannot pick up anything outside the tape.
    • The Gleaners are only allowed to gather grain outside the taped square. They cannot step inside the tape.
  2. Say: “Ready, set, HARVEST!”
  3. Let the children run and gather as much grain as they can into their baskets. It will go quickly.
  4. Call everyone back to the center and have them sit down.

Discussion

Ask the Harvesters: “Did you want to pick up the grain outside the square? Why did you have to leave it behind?”

Ask the Gleaners: “How did it feel to be able to pick up the grain left around the edges? Did it help you?”

Connection Back to the Bible Story

Explain: “In Bible times, God gave the Israelites a very special rule. When they were harvesting their crops, they were not allowed to harvest all the way to the edges of the field, and they weren’t allowed to pick up anything they dropped. They had to leave the leftovers for the poor people, the widows, and the foreigners traveling through. This was called ‘gleaning.’ It was God’s way of making sure everyone had food. Because Boaz obeyed this rule, Ruth was able to gather food to keep herself and Naomi alive!”

Craft Time

Activity Resource: Wheat Bundle Craft View Standalone →

Materials:

  • Yellow or green pipe cleaners (about 5 per child)
  • Yellow pony beads
  • Ribbon or yarn
  • Green construction paper (optional, for leaves)

Purpose

To give children a tactile experience of “gleaning” and creating a bundle of wheat, connecting them to Ruth’s hard work in the fields of Boaz.

Setup

  1. Count out 5-6 pipe cleaners in half if you want to save materials, or leave them full length for larger stalks of wheat.
  2. Put bowls of yellow pony beads on the tables.

Instructions

  1. The Grain: Give each child 5 pipe cleaners. Have them string 5-6 yellow pony beads onto the top of each pipe cleaner.
  2. Fold the very tip of the pipe cleaner down over the last bead so they don’t slide off!
  3. Slightly bend the beaded section at the top so it looks like the heavy, drooping head of a stalk of wheat.
  4. The Bundle: Have the children gather all 5 of their pipe cleaners together in a bunch.
  5. Give them a piece of ribbon or yarn to tie around the middle of the stalks, holding the bundle tightly together.
  6. (Optional) Let them cut a leaf shape out of green construction paper, write “God Provides” on it, and tie it into the bundle.

Discussion While Crafting

  • “Why did Ruth have to go into the fields to pick up leftover grain?” (Because she and Naomi were very poor and had no food).
  • “Did Ruth complain about having to work hard?” (No, she was faithful and worked all day long).
  • “Who owned the field and showed her incredible kindness?” (Boaz, the Kinsman-Redeemer).
  • “Every time you see this bundle of wheat, remember that God provided for Ruth, and He provides for us, too!”

Memory Verse

Ruth 1:16 (BSB)
“Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God.”

Practical Way to Teach:

  • Teach this verse using walking motions.
  • Take a big step forward on: “Where you go I will go”
  • Stop and plant your feet firmly on: “and where you stay I will stay.”
  • Point to the rest of the class on: “Your people will be my people”
  • Point up to heaven on: “and your God my God.”

Application

Being loyal doesn’t just mean sticking around when things are fun. This week, look for a way to be a loyal friend when it’s hard. If someone is sitting alone, sit with them. If someone is being made fun of, stand up for them. Choose to be a faithful friend like Ruth.

Take-Home Challenge

Boaz dropped extra grain on purpose so Ruth would find it. This week, try to do a “secret kindness” for someone in your family. Drop a little “extra grain” (do a chore without being asked, leave a nice note) and see what happens!

Closing Thought

The book of Ruth shows us that God uses ordinary people who make faithful choices. You might not feel like a king or a superhero, but when you are kind, loyal, and faithful to God, He uses your life to build a beautiful story. And best of all, the book of Ruth points us to Jesus—our perfect Redeemer who loved us enough to rescue us when we had nothing to offer Him in return.

Closing Prayer

“Heavenly Father, thank You for the beautiful story of Ruth. Thank You for showing us what true loyalty and kindness look like. But most of all, thank You for sending Jesus to be our perfect Kinsman-Redeemer. Thank You that Jesus came to rescue us from our sins. Help us to be loyal friends and to show Your kindness to the people around us this week. In Jesus’ name, Amen.”
